study.oneLine: You are handed a short phrase written in one alphabet and have to spell out the same phrase in another, using a wall of paired runes as your only dictionary.
study.whatYouSee: Twelve small tiles fill the top of the screen: six side-by-side pairs, cyan on the left, pink on the right, each tile carrying a different black rune, with a short dash joining the two tiles of a pair. Below a shaded divider sit two strips of five tiles, a cyan strip above and a pink strip below. Small brackets are clamped above and below one pink tile, and a thin bar runs along the very bottom edge.
study.firstMinute: Only four buttons do anything. Two slide the brackets left and right along the pink strip, so the brackets simply mark the slot you are currently editing. The other two cycle the rune inside that slot through a fixed loop of seven shapes. Nothing is ever confirmed, no tile tells you it is right, and every press — including just moving the brackets — eats into the bar at the bottom.
study.theRealisation: The six joined pairs up top are a dictionary, the cyan strip is a phrase in the left-hand alphabet, and your job is to write that phrase out in pink. The obvious reading — that pink is cyan turned or flipped — is the trap. Every rune sits at its own random angle, in the dictionary and in the strips alike, and the angles mean nothing at all: the pairings are arbitrary, so you can only look them up, never work them out.
study.whyItIsGood: Five slots times seven shapes, against a budget of roughly a hundred and thirty presses, with moving the cursor costing exactly as much as changing a rune — poking at it cannot work, so reading the dictionary is the only road through. The left tile of a pair always speaks for the top strip and the right tile for the bottom, even as the colours swap roles between levels, so the first lesson keeps paying. From there it climbs cleanly: straight swaps, then one rune becoming three, then three collapsing into one, then a phrase you must carry through a middle alphabet that is never drawn anywhere, and finally the flip where the brackets leave the strips, climb into the pair grid and widen to grip a whole dictionary entry. When you finish, the game replays your sentence piece by piece, lighting each chunk and outlining the dictionary entry that justified it.
study.portableIdea: Late in a game, freeze both the question and the answer and let the player edit the rulebook instead. Same board, same four buttons, opposite direction of thought: rather than applying the rules you were given, you repair a broken set of rules until it produces the answer already sitting on screen. A multi-slot entry moves as one block, so the shapes inside it keep their spacing — which quietly becomes a constraint the player has to plan around.
study.ourGap: Our games hand the player a rule and ask them to execute it; not one of ours ever hands the rule itself over to be rewritten, so the player is always solving inside the system and never repairing it. We also let a button-masher stumble into the answer, where this one prices every single press so tightly that reading the board is cheaper than trying things.
study.uncertain: The middle alphabet in the two-hop levels is never drawn on screen anywhere, so I am inferring the player is meant to hold that step entirely in their head. I could not confirm that by playing.

verdict.wrongClaims:
Four claims the source contradicts.

1. "A middle alphabet that is never drawn anywhere" — this is backwards, and it is the one thing he flagged as unverified. There are three tile colours in this game, not two: cyan, pink and yellow. On the two-hop level all three are on screen at once. The wall of pairs holds cyan-to-pink entries and pink-to-yellow entries side by side in the same grid. The question strip is cyan and the answer strip is yellow. Pink appears nowhere in either strip — only in the dictionary. That mismatch IS the level's tell: the colour you can see in the rulebook but not on either strip is the colour you have to route through. Nothing is held in the head; every pink glyph you need is printed in front of you. The victory replay confirms it — on that level it outlines four tiles per chunk: the cyan one, the pink one it becomes, the pink one on the other entry, and the yellow one it ends as. It draws the whole route.

2. The description knows only two alphabets. There are three, seven glyphs each, twenty-one shapes in all, and no shape is shared between them. They rotate roles level to level: cyan into pink, then pink into yellow, then yellow into cyan. "The colours swap roles between levels" badly undersells a third alphabet.

3. The level ladder is misordered and stops one level early. There are six levels. The flip — brackets leaving the strips and climbing into the dictionary — is the fifth, not the finale. The sixth is the real ending, and it is the flip AND the two-hop chain AND one-glyph-becomes-two all at once, on a rulebook of six half-broken entries. It is also the only level with a bigger allowance. The write-up makes the game sound like it peaks one step before it actually does.

4. "One rune becoming three, then three collapsing into one" is not the shape of those two levels. The second level only ever expands — its entries run one-to-one, one-to-two and one-to-three, never the other way. The third mixes freely in both directions: one-to-one, one-to-two, two-to-one, two-to-two, and a single three-to-one. So the third level's lesson is not collapse, it is that word boundaries no longer line up with tiles on either strip, and the two strips no longer even hold the same number of tiles.

Plus a wrong explanation of why the game works. He says it "prices every single press so tightly that reading the board is cheaper than trying things." The allowance is actually roomy — several times what an informed solve costs on every level, and roughly double what a reference solve spends. What stops mashing is that the game never answers: no tick on a correct tile, no partial credit, no warmer-or-colder. The board stays silent until every glyph in the line is right at once, then simply ends.

Smaller: the bracket grips one half of a dictionary entry, not a whole entry, and it visits the input halves too — so you can redefine what a rule matches, not just what it produces. The cursor wraps, so it is a ring, not a track with ends. "Six pairs" and "five slots" are the opening screen only; other levels give eight pairs or four, and seven slots or six. The victory replay lights both strips together, not just the answer.
verdict.correctedOneLine: You are handed a short phrase in one alphabet and have to spell it out in another, reading a wall of paired runes as your only dictionary — later levels route you through a third alphabet that appears only in the dictionary and never in the phrase, then freeze the phrase and hand you the dictionary to repair instead.

study.oneLine: You float upward through a flooded stone shaft, steering only left and right, dissolving the ceilings that pin you down until you reach the prize at the top.
study.whatYouSee: A tall shaft of dark stone, freckled with a few pale dots, with wide pale-blue channels carved through it like flooded corridors. The blue is empty space, not a substance — the flooded look is entirely paint, and those freckles are the only genuinely decorative thing on this screen. Green blocks sit in the channels, one in a solid three-by-three clump and one in a wide shelf; your marker is a small blue blob with a bright fin, sitting low in the middle, and a thin bar runs along the very bottom edge with a short coloured stub at its left end.
study.firstMinute: You press right and just slide one cell over. You press right again, and again, still only sliding sideways. On the fourth press you don't slide — you shoot up three rows and stop with a thud beneath the green shelf, the whole view scrolling up to follow you. Then you click the green block directly over your head, it shrinks away in three quick frames, and you rise again; every press so far has widened that bar at the bottom by a hair, and when it reaches the far edge you are out of moves.
study.theRealisation: There is no up button. You rise on your own the moment nothing is directly over your head, so pressing left and right isn't walking — it's hunting for the gap in the ceiling. The blue doesn't carry you anywhere; you are simply buoyant in it, and from that point on every move is a question about what is above you rather than what is beside you.
study.whyItIsGood: You are given only left, right, click and undo, so height is always a consequence and never a command — which is exactly what floating feels like. In the early levels something is rising from below, off-screen when you start, and it only gains on you during moves where you failed to rise: shuffling sideways under a ceiling costs you, a move that lifts you is free. So the game applies real pressure without ever punishing you for thinking, only for being lost. Later it plays a second trick — the specks and strips you had written off as wallpaper turn out to be the controls: see-through shapes you swim straight through go solid when clicked, and a decorative-looking band set into the rock flips which way is down.
study.portableIdea: Make the pressure clock advance only on moves where the player failed to make progress, never on every turn. A wasted step costs time; a step that gets you somewhere is free. It reads as generous rather than punishing, it lets a player stop and think without bleeding, and it silently teaches them what the game counts as progress — no tutorial text needed.
study.ourGap: Almost all our games hand the player four directions plus a confirm on a fixed single-screen board, so every cell of movement is something the player asked for and nothing is ever done to them — no drift, no buoyancy, no sense of a world with physics of its own. Where we do run a clock it ticks on every action, which punishes thinking exactly as hard as it punishes flailing, and our scenery is genuinely inert rather than quietly load-bearing.
study.uncertain: Colour names here come from the screenshot description, not from me — I read palette slots, not hues. Two things I inferred rather than confirmed: the two mirror-image hazard shapes both kill on contact, so their flipped orientation appears purely cosmetic, drawn so the dangerous face points at whichever side you would arrive from, but I cannot prove that was the intent; and I believe undo rewinds the rising tide along with the rest of the board while leaving the spent move bar spent, though I only traced that the whole board gets snapshotted, not the tide specifically. I am also assuming the screenshot is the first level a few moves in, just after the player has floated up once — that is the only camera position where a three-by-three clump and a wide shelf are both on screen at the same time.

verdict.wrongClaims:
THE BIG ONE — THE TAKEAWAY IS BUILT ON A FALSE PREMISE.

That bar along the bottom is a flat move budget, and it advances on every single press. Click on empty water: a notch. Click on bare rock: a notch. Press undo: a notch, on top of the one you just undid. Nothing gives a notch back except restarting the level, which throws away everything you had done. Fill the bar and you lose the level outright — sixty-four presses in the first six levels, a hundred and twenty-eight in the last three, where it fills once in one colour and then again in a second. So the game absolutely does punish thinking, on every action, in all nine levels. The generous clock he admires is real, but it is the SECONDARY pressure and it runs in only the first three levels. Both the "portable idea" and the "our gap" paragraph assert that this game never ticks per turn. It ticks per turn everywhere. The lesson he pulled out is a good lesson; it just is not this game's.

Related: undo does not merely "leave the spent move bar spent." It spends another notch of it. Rewinding costs the same as acting.

"THE PRIZE AT THE TOP" IS WRONG IN FOUR OF THE NINE LEVELS.

In levels four, six, seven and nine the prize sits BELOW where you start. Getting to it means reversing your drift and sinking down to it. Rising is the first third of this game, not its shape.

DISSOLVING CEILINGS IS NOT THE THROUGH-LINE EITHER.

The green blocks vanish completely from levels six, seven and eight. By then the puzzle is made of reversers and see-through blocks, and clearing a ceiling is barely part of it.

THE SEE-THROUGH BLOCKS ARE A SWITCH, NOT A ONE-WAY SOLIDIFIER.

He is right that clicking a ghosted one hardens it, and in levels six and seven — which are stuffed with them — hardening one into a landing pad is exactly the point. But it runs both ways: click a SOLID one and it ghosts, opening a channel you drift straight through. Levels eight and nine contain only solid ones, so that second direction is the whole late game, and it is absent from his account.

A WHOLE CLICKABLE TYPE IS MISSING.

There is a block that, when clicked, vanishes and immediately plants a copy of itself in every empty cell beside it, above it and below it. One click turns one obstacle into as many as four, spreading outward. It appears in the last two levels and he never mentions it.

THE HAZARDS DO NOT KILL ON CONTACT.

Walking sideways into one is a harmless bump — it acts as a plain wall and you stay put. They only kill when you DRIFT into one: when the thing that stops your rise, or your fall once you have reversed, is a hazard. Which face you meet is the face your drift runs into. That actually makes his guess about the mirrored orientations better than he thought: the two shapes are exact vertical mirrors of each other and behave identically, so the flip is purely cosmetic.

THE RISING MASS GAINS ABOUT HALF AS OFTEN AS HE SAYS.

He has the rule right in kind — it never advances on a press that lifts you. But it advances at most every other action: a wasted press only pushes it up when your running press count happens to be even, and clicks never push it at all, not even a click that achieves nothing.

TWO SMALL ONES.

You do not rise "the moment" nothing is over your head. Rising is resolved as part of a press. Click a block that is not the one directly overhead and it clears while you stay exactly where you are, until you move.

The direction-reverser is not decorative. It is the same bold rounded tile as the dissolving blocks, in red, and it arrives in level four as scattered single tiles. The stripe-set-into-the-rock layout he describes only shows up in the last couple of levels.

WHAT CHECKS OUT — AND MOST OF IT DOES.

The control set is exactly right: left, right, click, undo, and no up. The core realisation is right: you drift on your own, sideways pressing is hunting for the gap, height is never a command. The opening beat is right to the letter — three sideways slides, then on the fourth press a float of exactly three rows onto a four-wide green shelf, with the three-by-three green clump nearby, and a click overhead that shrinks the block away in three frames. His guess that the screenshot is level one just after the first float is correct; that is the camera position where both shapes are on screen. The rising mass exists only in the early levels and does start off-screen below. Undo does rewind the board including the rising mass and the current drift direction. And his colour reading, which he flagged as borrowed, is right: empty space is pale blue, the rock is black with grey freckles, the dissolving blocks are green, the player is a blue blob with a yellow marker on its facing side, the prize is a small pink cross.
verdict.correctedOneLine: You drift automatically — upward at first — and can only steer left and right, so the game is about clicking the blocks in your path to clear them, harden them, or reverse which way you drift, until you reach the prize, which in the later levels lies below you rather than above, and always before the move meter along the bottom edge fills up.

study.oneLine: A crate-hauling game that uses Sokoban's verbs and then deliberately throws away Sokoban's tension: you can always pull, so nothing is ever ruined, and the only thing you can actually lose is time.
study.whatYouSee: An almost empty field. In the middle sits a framed strip of floor three cells wide; scattered around it are three small framed squares, and near the bottom a little block with a lip on one edge. A thin bar runs the full width of the very bottom of the screen, filled end to end. No text, no counters, no legend.
study.firstMinute: You press a direction and move exactly one cell, and the lip on your block swings round to face that way, so you learn it is a pointer rather than decoration. Step next to a crate and its frame lights up before you have touched it. Press the fifth key and the frame changes again: it is yours now, and every step you take, it takes with you. Two more steps and it is sitting in the marked strip; press the fifth key to let go, and the board ends the moment the last crate is parked and nobody is holding it.
study.theRealisation: The crate is not pushed, it rides. It keeps whatever position it had at the moment you grabbed it and can never change sides, because you cannot turn while carrying, which means you can drag it behind you or walk sideways with it alongside you. The opening board's obvious first move happens to be a push, so a player can clear several boards still believing this is a push-only game.
study.whyItIsGood: Three boards in, a dotted line runs the full height of the map. You cannot cross it, but a crate can be parked on it, and on the far side there is a unit doing your job for you: it walks to loose crates and carries them to the marked floor, one cell for every key you press. You can never reach each other, so the wall stops being a wall and becomes a counter you slide goods across. Later a second unit appears that does the identical thing toward the wrong bay, will lift a crate straight out of your hands, and lights up when you face it, because facing it and pressing that same fifth key destroys it, while the helpful one never changes appearance at all.
study.portableIdea: Put a worker on the board that wants exactly what the player wants and can achieve it without them, and its mirror image that hauls the same crates to the wrong place. Both move one cell for every key the player presses, so neither can outrun the player or fall behind. Once someone is standing on the far side, a barrier that stops people but not cargo stops being a dead drop and becomes a hand-off counter — the same trick one of our games already has, but with nobody over there to receive.
study.ourGap: Our push-block games are solitaire against a fixed world: nothing on our boards wants anything, so every level has a single plan you work out once and then execute, and our only moving parts walk fixed loops that never touch a crate. But the Boss's premise is wrong in the other direction, so the gap is narrower than he thinks — wa30 forgives every move and therefore has no dead corners and no restart-I-killed-it moment, which is the exact tension our four are built on.
study.uncertain: I could not run it, so three things are inference. What happens when the bar empties: I know it is a loss, not whether it restarts the board or ends the run. Whether any shipped board can actually strand the helpful unit holding a crate it has no route to deliver — the rules permit it, and the player's only remedy is to take the crate off it. And the hand-off reading of the divided boards is worked out from the geometry and the movement rules, not observed in play, though the geometry leaves no other way to finish them.

verdict.wrongClaims:
Three things are wrong, one of them badly.

1) "A second unit that does the identical thing toward the wrong bay." Not identical — the thief is far nastier than its mirror. The helpful unit only ever touches crates lying loose and undelivered: it will not take one out of anybody's hands, and it will not touch a crate already sitting on marked floor. The thief has neither restraint. It lifts cargo out of your hands AND out of the helper's hands, and nothing stops it walking up to floor you already finished and hauling that crate back off it. So a board is never banked until the last crate lands and the thief is gone. That is exactly the tension he says the game threw away, and a designer building from his description would build the placid half and miss it.

2) "Step next to a crate and its frame lights up." Proximity is not the trigger — facing is. The outline only changes on the crate your lip is pointed at. It is not a warmth glow, it is the game telling you what the fifth key will act on, which is the same signal the thief gives when it lights up. One highlight language, not two.

3) "The player's only remedy is to take the crate off it." True only where you can reach the helper, and on the divided boards the design specifically forbids that. On the third board the line runs wall to wall; on the fourth you are sealed inside a closed ring of it. A helper stranded out there holding a crate cannot be relieved. The board just runs down.

Small thing he missed, and the tidiest: the fifth key is overloaded and hands always win. With a crate in hand it drops, never strikes — you cannot kill the thief while carrying anything. The moment it robs you is the moment you can hit back.

RESOLVED, not errors — his three flagged unknowns land in his favour.
- Running the bar dry restarts the current board only. Everything you already cleared stays cleared. It costs you the board, not the run. The bar also refills at every board, and the budgets are per-board and deliberately mean: the second board gives you about seventy presses, nowhere near enough to fetch five crates across the map yourself. That is how the game forces you to notice the helper.
- The hand-off reading is not inference — it is mandatory on two boards. The third has no marked floor at all on your side of the line. The fourth seals you inside a closed ring with every scrap of marked floor outside it and three helpers out there; you cannot deliver a single crate yourself, only slide them onto the ring and let the helpers collect. He worked that out from geometry alone and got it exactly right.
- And the helper has no rule against the wrong bay either. It will go and fetch crates the thief dumped there and carry them where they belong. It is a counter-agent, not just free labour.
verdict.correctedOneLine: A crate-hauling game that uses Sokoban's verbs and then relocates Sokoban's tension rather than discarding it: you can always pull, so no move ever ruins a board, but a thief works the same crates in reverse — taking them out of your hands and off the floor you already delivered them to — so the pressure shifts from "did I wreck this" to "can I out-pace the thing undoing my work," and the clock is still the only way to actually lose.

study.oneLine: Two metal parts with marked contact points, and you turn and slide them until every marked point on one is covered by its partner on the other.
study.whatYouSee: A pale blue field with two pieces on it: left, a white bracket like a squared-off staple with two legs; right, a green rectangular ring. Two small red squares sit at the tips of the bracket's legs, and two more hug the outside of the ring's left wall, one pair per piece. The bracket looks white only because you are holding it — put it down and it turns orange, and whichever piece you pick up next goes white instead.
study.firstMinute: Arrow keys slide the piece you are holding one cell at a time, and a turn button spins it a quarter turn; the pieces pass straight through each other, so this is alignment, not packing. Clicking a different piece picks that one up instead — it goes white, and the one you put down shows its real colour again. Nothing you do changes the red squares until two of them land on the same cell, and then both go dark grey and stay that way. The bar across the top is a move budget, and the white part is moves already spent, so it eats inward from the left as you work.
study.theRealisation: The red squares are not finished welds, they are the joints still to make — red is the to-do list, and a joint goes dark grey the moment it is done. Read that way they are a checklist printed onto the pieces: every red cell must be covered by another piece's red cell, and rotation and position stop being a search and become a calculation. The sting is that there are two kinds of red dot, identical to look at, and each only counts against its own kind — so a join can look finished, both dots gone dark and the parts locked together, and the level still won't clear because the piece is on backwards.
study.whyItIsGood: Every move pays. A dot goes out the instant it is right, so you are never guessing whether you are closer, and the whole win condition is drawn on the board and countable — no legend, no goal text, no hidden rule. Later levels keep exactly those rules and just take away information: everything except the piece in your hand goes black, and some pieces grow or shrink a segment at a time, each new segment bringing its own dot to satisfy, so the number of dots on the fixed pieces quietly tells you how long to make the adjustable one. And it ends well — the last dot goes dark, the two parts read as one continuous object, and you get a beat to look at it before the next level loads.
study.portableIdea: Print the win condition onto the pieces themselves, as a per-cell checklist that goes out one mark at a time. No legend and no goal text: the player can always count how much is left and see which specific cell is still wrong, so every single move returns a verdict instead of silence.
study.ourGap: Our games hide the rule and grade per room — you either open the door or you don't, and a wrong hypothesis returns nothing at all, so the player wanders. This one shows the goal completely, hides only the arrangement, and pays out per connector, which makes wandering almost impossible.
study.uncertain: I could not run it, so this is reconstructed from the source and the level layouts. Two inferences: that the mismatched-join trap is used deliberately in the later levels (I only confirmed it is reachable), and how the growing pieces read in motion. One correction to the screenshot rather than an uncertainty — a single white segment on the top bar means two or three moves spent out of a generous budget, so that shot is right at the start of level one, not near the end of it.

verdict.wrongClaims:
FOUR THINGS THAT ARE ACTUALLY WRONG

1. "Both go dark grey and stay that way." They do not stay. The dark grey is a live readout, not a latch. Slide a joined piece one cell apart and both marks snap straight back to red. I did exactly that and watched them flip. Nothing in this game is ever banked — the board only ever tells you about right now. That is arguably a better mechanic than the one described, but it is not the one described, and it changes the feel completely: you can undo your own progress by accident.

2. The turn button does not turn the pieces that grow. On an adjustable piece, that same button lengthens and shortens it instead — up to full length, then back down again, bouncing rather than wrapping round. Those pieces can never be rotated at all; they are frozen at the angle they start in, and they always grow out from the same corner. The sting is the timing: the first level with an adjustable piece hands you that piece already in your hand, so the button that has meant "turn" for four levels silently means "resize" on your very first press. There is also a small white pip on the adjustable piece that does the same job when you click it, and the pip disappears once the piece is at full length — the game quietly telling you there is nothing more to give.

3. The later levels do not dim the other pieces. They rub the checklist off them. From the third level on, every part except the one in your hand is a flat charcoal silhouette — right shape, one colour, and no marks on it whatsoever. Not black, and not "everything goes dark but you can still read it": the red dots on the other pieces are gone. Only the piece you are holding shows its real colour and its own marks. So you have to pick each part up in turn just to find out what it still needs. This is the note worth taking away, because the report's own lesson contradicts it. "The player can always count how much is left" is true for two levels out of six. The arc runs the opposite way to the portable idea as written: the game opens with the whole win condition printed on the board, then takes the printing away, and the per-move payout survives only on the piece in your hand.

4. "Each new segment bringing its own dot" is invented as a rule. It holds for the first adjustable piece. On the last level there are two adjustable pieces, and one of them carries the same three marks at every length — it just gets longer. You cannot count your way to its length; you have to fit it. The "count the marks on the fixed pieces and that tells you how long to make it" trick works cleanly exactly once, on one puzzle, and then the game stops honouring it.

SMALLER CORRECTIONS

- The one-line says "two metal parts". Only the first level has two. After that it is three, then four, and on the last level five, two of them adjustable.
- Clicking the piece you are already holding puts it down and leaves you holding nothing at all. Arrows and the turn button then do nothing — but they still spend moves off the bar. Easy to sit there pressing keys and bleeding budget.
- Running the bar out is a loss. The run ends there; it is not just a nag.
- "A pale blue field" is level one only. The field colour changes every level — orange, blue, purple — and it is one of the few signals that you have moved on.

TWO UPGRADES RATHER THAN REFUTATIONS

- The mismatched-join trap is not a late-level curiosity that is merely "reachable". It is live on the very first puzzle and it is close to a coin flip. Only two of the four orientations put the two marks on the right axis, and one of those two is the trap: the pieces nest perfectly, both marks go dark grey, and nothing happens. I walked into it deliberately and the level just sat there. State it as fact, not inference.
- The trap does not ramp. One of the middle levels has no second kind of mark anywhere in it, so it is completely trap-free. The deception comes and goes level by level.

WHAT HE GOT RIGHT, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING

The two kinds of mark really are drawn in two shades of red that come out identical on screen — a deliberate deception in the art, and he called it without ever running the game. The bar really does fill white from the left as you spend, white being spent. His screenshot correction is exact: one white segment on that bar is two or three moves gone out of the first level's budget. And the whole level-one picture holds up — the white bracket that turns orange the moment you put it down, the green ring, the marks sitting at the tips of the bracket's legs and hugging the outside of the ring's left wall, and the pieces sliding straight through one another. The central realisation — red is the to-do list, grey is done, and the win condition is printed on the parts — is correct.
verdict.correctedOneLine: A handful of metal parts stamped with red joint marks; you pick one up and slide, turn or stretch it until every mark sits under a matching mark on another part — and some marks that look identical are secretly not.

study.oneLine: A little green walker has to reach a yellow square, but most of the floor between them doesn't exist yet — you build the path by pressing coloured buttons on a panel that reshape tiles right across the board.
study.whatYouSee: A dark board, framed by wide grey bands top and bottom, with a dotted white line running down the right-hand third. Left of the line, a small green square and a small yellow square sit on separate grey pads, with a few coloured blocks stranded in the space between them — a long red bar lying flat, a solid blue square, a fuzzy blue checkerboard. Right of the line, on black, two flat-topped shapes, one red and one blue, each ringed in a thick white outline.
study.firstMinute: You press the arrows and the green square rattles around inside a grey pad about three steps wide. Every direction is a wall, and nothing else on the board reacts. So you click one of the shapes on the right — its white outline pops off for good, and away across the board a blue tile that was a fuzzy checkerboard turns solid, opening the way up. From there you settle into a rhythm: walk as far as the floor goes, press a button, walk again.
study.theRealisation: The two shapes on the right are not targets to copy. They are buttons, and each is the colour of the pieces it controls — press the red one and the long red bar lying flat swings upright into a ladder that reaches the goal. The screenshot we were sent is that exact moment: the red bar standing tall with the checkered tile at its top and the green man at its foot, white outlines already gone. He had built the staircase and didn't know it.
study.whyItIsGood: Pieces never blink in and out — they pivot, slide, or grow in from both ends, so you can read where the floor is heading before you commit, and a checkerboard always means "half-missing, no footing." Get it wrong and the screen irises to black around you, rewinds you one move and charges twenty off your budget; it never kills you outright, it just makes it expensive, so you keep experimenting. The panel keeps growing too: later buttons start locked, and you go fetch a small coloured token on foot to make one appear in the empty slot waiting for it. And in the last level the walkway simply runs straight through the dotted line with the goal on the far side — the divider you spent five levels treating as a wall turns out not to be one.
study.portableIdea: When you reshape a platform, you have to already be standing on the part of it that survives the change — otherwise the ground goes out from under you. That turns every button press into a positioning problem: not just "should I press this" but "where do I need to be standing first."
study.ourGap: Nearly all our games are arrow-keys only; the pointer barely features, and everything a player can affect is under their feet or one step away. We have nothing with a separate control surface that acts at a distance, nothing that grows or unlocks as you play, and by our own audit most of our games can't end a run at all — so a wrong press costs nothing and there is never anything to be careful with.
study.uncertain: One button in the last level cycles a small tile through four colours; I traced the colour changing but could find nothing that depends on it, so I may have missed its purpose. The two grey bands are just framing where the board is shorter than the screen (they vanish in the taller later levels) — the hair-thin white line along the very bottom edge is a separate thing, the move budget, eaten away from the left. My comparison to our own games rests on a quick scan (most of ours never read a click at all) plus our existing audit, not a game-by-game review.

verdict.correctedOneLine: A little green walker has to reach a yellow square, but most of the floor between them doesn't exist yet — you build the path by pressing buttons on a side panel that reshape platforms right across the board, and in the later levels you also drive a claw along a painted track to fetch and carry pieces, and stand on coloured pads that fling you across the level to their matching twin.
verdict.wrongClaims:
I could run this one, so everything below is something I watched happen, not something I inferred.

WHAT HE GOT RIGHT — and it is a lot. The premise, the opening screen, the two flat-topped shapes being buttons, the red bar swinging upright when you press red, the checkerboard meaning "you can't stand here", the way the failure works (the walker dissolves, the screen irises to black around it, you get put back exactly one move and charged twenty off the meter), the hair-thin white line along the very bottom that gets eaten from the left, the grey bands being letterboxing that disappears once the boards get taller, fetching a small coloured morsel on foot to make a missing button appear in the gap waiting for it, and the last level's walkway running straight through the dotted line with the goal sitting on the far side. All confirmed. His portable idea is confirmed too — I solved the first level and the whole thing turns on standing on the corner of the red bar that survives the swing.

But the second half of the game is missing, and what is in its place is wrong.

1. THE CLAW. From the fifth level the panel is not more colour buttons. It grows a row of four small arrow buttons and a red bar, and those drive a big red claw that lives on the board, riding a white track painted across the floor. Press an arrow and the claw slides four squares along the track — twice as far as the walker moves. Park it over the tall orange pillar, press the red bar, and it clamps shut on the pillar; from then on the pillar goes wherever the claw goes, and the walker stands on it wherever you leave it. The claw only goes where the paint goes, so getting it anywhere is a routing puzzle in itself. Describing this as "later buttons start locked" turns a second driveable machine into more of the same.

2. THE WARP PADS. From the third level onward there are small coloured pads scattered around the board, two or more of a colour. Stand on one, press the panel button of that colour, and the walker is thrown clean across the level to the matching pad. Press it again and you come back. I did exactly this and watched him jump corner to corner. It is in four of the six levels and the write-up never mentions it once.

3. THE FOUR-COLOUR SQUARE IS THE WARP'S STEERING — which is the thing he flagged as unexplained. In the last level one of those pads can be re-coloured by a panel button that is itself a swatch of all four colours. Whatever colour the pad is wearing decides where the warp sends you: wearing pink it sends you to the pink pad, yellow to the yellow one in the far corner, blue to the blue one down below. Set it to red and nothing at all happens, because that level has no red twin — which is almost certainly why he traced the colour changing and saw nothing depend on it. He was one press away.

4. BUTTONS DO BLINK IN AND OUT, and the panel does not only grow. In the last level there is a little cross of four pads on the floor down in a corner, each with a coloured pip. On the panel there is a matching cross of four dark, empty sockets, each carrying the same coloured pip. Step onto the pad with the purple pip and the purple socket fills in solid and becomes the claw's up-button. Step off and it goes dark again. Four of the panel's controls only exist while the walker is standing on the right square of floor. That is a lovely idea, and it is the exact opposite of "the panel keeps growing".

5. "EACH IS THE COLOUR OF THE PIECES IT CONTROLS" stops being true. It holds for the two buttons in the first level, and for the pink pads later. But from the fourth level the game deliberately crosses the wires: a plain grey square button drives an orange bar, and a yellow L-shaped button drives a pale grey block that slides. Take the colour rule as law there and you press the wrong one.

6. BOTH WHITE OUTLINES POP OFF AT ONCE, not just the one you clicked. The first press of either button strips the ring from both. It reads as a one-time "you've got it" for the whole panel.

7. THE BLUE BUTTON IS A SEE-SAW, NOT A SWITCH. It does not simply turn a checkerboard solid. It flips both blue squares at the same time — the one near you fills in and the one up beside the goal hollows out. That is why the first level needs blue pressed twice: once to get out of the starting pad, and again later, after you have walked past it, to re-open the square next to the goal. (If the screenshot really shows the red bar upright with a checkered square at its top, that state is one press short of a finished path, not a finished one — that checkered square is the last step and it is a wall.)

8. A FALL CAN END THE RUN. The twenty-move charge and the one-move rewind are both right, but if you have fewer than twenty moves left the fall is fatal and the game is over on the spot. The run also ends flatly when the meter empties. "It never kills you outright" is not quite true.

9. Worth knowing for the budget: pressing a button costs two moves off the meter, walking a step costs one. Pressing is the expensive action.

study.oneLine: Peg solitaire in a strangely shaped room: hop green pieces over each other until only one is left, and on later levels ride a piece between rooms on a little cart.
study.whatYouSee: A cyan field with one black-outlined room sitting on it, shaped like a fat L and tiled white and grey. Five green pieces sit on the floor in no pattern. The room casts a thin blue shadow along two of its edges, which is the only thing making it read as an object on a table rather than a pattern on a screen; a pale bar runs across the very top, barely started, and the counter says level one of ten.
study.firstMinute: You click a green piece. A dark ring snaps around it, and grey donuts appear on the empty floor two squares away, in every direction you are actually allowed to go. Click a donut and the piece arcs across, and the piece it passed over shrinks and pops out of existence. Click a piece that has no legal hop and it just shudders and refuses to select.
study.theRealisation: It is peg solitaire. Every hop eats the piece you hopped over, so the green pieces are not things to collect, they are things to spend, and you have won when one is left. On level one there are only two possible opening moves, and one of them quietly makes the level unwinnable.
study.whyItIsGood: The button is not a move-confirm. Pressing it restarts the level, and it arrives in three beats: first every remaining green piece turns grey and jitters side to side, so the board itself tells you it is over; then nothing happens for about two thirds of a second; then a purple button on a post rises up from below the bottom edge and eases to a stop in the bottom-left corner. The whole bottom-left corner is clickable, not just the button art, and on level one, if you click anywhere useless after it has arrived, a blue ring pulses right on top of it. Nothing else in the game ever moves onto the screen from outside, so its arrival is unmistakable even though it is never explained.
study.portableIdea: When the player breaks a puzzle, do not leave them stewing and do not leave a dead button sitting on screen from the start. Make the control an event: the board reacts first, then a beat of silence, then the control physically walks in from off-screen and settles. And you do not need a solver to know when to fire it — this game simply hand-lists the handful of squares that kill each early level and triggers on those. That is a week of authoring, not a month of engineering.
study.ourGap: None of our games have a confirm step at all: every action commits the instant it is pressed, and nothing in the set shows you which moves are legal before you take one. We also have no control that appears only when it is needed — whatever is on screen at the start is on screen forever — so a button arriving can never mean anything to our players.
study.uncertain: The screenshot shows four green pieces but level one opens with five, so that shot was probably taken after the first correct hop, which also fits the barely-moved bar. I am also inferring that the dead-end detector only covers levels one, two, three and six; on the rest you can strand yourself and no button ever comes, you just burn the meter down and lose.

verdict.wrongClaims:
He got a lot right, but four load-bearing mechanics are stated wrongly.

1. NOT EVERY HOP EATS THE PIECE YOU JUMP. Only a piece of your own colour is taken. The boards are also seeded with little purple blocks, and later with a red piece and with blue pieces. All of those are perfectly legal to jump over and none of them ever disappears — they are permanent stepping stones. When you hop something of a different colour, your piece visibly passes over the top of it and the thing is still standing when you land. So "the green pieces are things to spend" is only half of it: a good part of what is on the floor exists purely to be vaulted, again and again. This is the single biggest error, because it is the sentence the whole "theRealisation" paragraph rests on.

2. "YOU HAVE WON WHEN ONE IS LEFT" IS NOT ALWAYS THE GOAL. On the sixth and seventh levels the level is complete when TWO pieces remain. Each of those two levels holds a single red piece that nothing can ever capture, so the finish line is "the red one, plus one green one." On the last three levels the blue pieces do not count toward the goal at all — you clear the greens down to one and the blues just stay standing where they are.

3. IT IS NOT A CLICK-ONLY GAME. There are six controls. Four of them are direction buttons. Pressing one shifts every orange cart tile on the board one square along its rails, carrying whatever is standing on it — and if more than one cart is on the board, they all move at once. So you do not "ride" the cart by clicking; you park it, hop a piece onto it, then drive it with the direction buttons, and pressing a direction also cancels whatever piece you had selected. This starts on the SECOND level, not on "later levels" — the cart arrives the moment level one is done.

4. THERE IS AN UNDO, AND IT IS AVAILABLE THE WHOLE TIME. One of the six controls steps the entire board back one action, as many times as you like. That flatly kills the closing guess in "uncertain": on the levels with no dead-end detector you do not "just burn the meter down and lose" — you back up and try again. It also softens the "do not leave them stewing" lesson, because the player was never actually stuck; the button is a convenience on top of a rewind that was always there.

5. THE BLUE RING ON LEVEL ONE IS A TUTORIAL POINTER, AND IT IS THERE FROM THE FIRST CLICK. Click anywhere useless on level one before you have moved, and the ring pulses directly on the one piece you are supposed to pick up. Select that piece and click uselessly again, and the ring moves to the exact square you are supposed to land on. Only once the restart button has arrived does the ring switch to pulsing over the button. He caught the third of those three cases and missed the first two, which is a pity — the two-stage "here, now here" pointer is the more interesting piece of design.

6. THE BEATS OF THE FAILURE SEQUENCE ARE IN THE WRONG ORDER. The dead pause comes FIRST, not in the middle. What actually happens: you land on the fatal square, and for about half a second nothing whatever happens — the board just sits there looking normal. Then the remaining pieces go grey and shiver. Then, almost immediately after that, the button comes up. The silence he places between the shiver and the button belongs in front of the grey-out. Worth noting too: it fires the instant you land on the killing square, before you have had any chance to flail about discovering you are stuck — which is a stronger version of the point he was making.

7. THE BUTTON DOES NOT EASE TO A STOP, IT BOUNCES. It shoots up from below the bottom edge, overshoots, drops back, and settles with a couple of visible bounces, like something spring-loaded shoved up through the floor. "Eases to a stop" describes a different, calmer arrival than the one that is there.

8. "NOTHING ELSE IN THE GAME EVER MOVES ONTO THE SCREEN FROM OUTSIDE" IS FALSE. From the third level onward the whole board slides sideways whenever a cart crosses between rooms, and entire rooms travel in from off-screen. It holds for the first two levels only. The button's entrance is still distinctive, but not for the reason he gives.

SMALL STUFF, IN PASSING. Hops are strictly up, down, left and right — never diagonal, so there are only ever four grey donuts on offer. The level-one room is not an L: it is a wide bar across the top with a narrow column dropping from its right-hand end, closer to a 7. The floor is off-white squares separated by white lines rather than white and grey; the contrast is far lower than "white and grey" implies, which is exactly why the cart tiles shout when they turn up — they are bright orange. And the strip along the top is a running tally of every button you press, not a budget you can win back: hitting the restart button does not wind it back.

WHAT HE GOT RIGHT, AND IT IS A LOT. Five pieces on level one — correct. Exactly two possible opening moves, one of which quietly kills the level — correct, and I checked the resulting position; you really are stranded with four pieces and nothing to do. The guess that the dead-end warning covers only levels one, two, three and six is exactly right, and that is a genuinely good call from a screenshot. The whole bottom-left corner being clickable rather than just the button art — right. Restart rather than move-confirm — right. The dark ring snapping around a selected piece, the grey donuts appearing two squares out, the shudder when you click a piece with no legal hop, the jumped piece shrinking away to nothing, the thin blue shadow along two edges of the room, and the fact that the fatal squares are hand-listed rather than found by a solver — all correct.
verdict.correctedOneLine: Peg solitaire in oddly shaped rooms: hop a piece over another of its own colour to take it — off-colour pieces and purple blocks stay put as permanent stepping stones — until one piece is left (two, on a couple of levels), and from the second level on drive little rail carts with the direction buttons to ferry a piece from room to room.

_brief:
# What we're missing

Our games are correct and legible, which is most of the job. What separates them is that every one of ours states its single idea in the first ten seconds and never revises it. The official games are built around a moment where the player's model breaks — you discover there is no up button, that the wall you can't cross has a worker on the other side of it, that the button which has meant "turn" for four levels now means "stretch." They get that out of four to six controls, not out of more content. They add meanings rather than buttons, and they raise difficulty by changing what the player can *see* rather than by enlarging the board. That's the gap. It isn't art, theme, or variety.

# The recurring shapes

**One button, many meanings.** In the connector game the turn button silently becomes a stretch button the first time you hold a piece that grows; in the crate game the same key drops your cargo when your hands are full and destroys a thief when they're empty. The control set never grows, so every new meaning is learned by pressing a key you already trusted.

**The world moves without you.** In the floating game you steer only left and right and rise on your own, so pressing sideways isn't walking — it's hunting for the gap in the ceiling. Elsewhere a claw rides a painted track, coloured pads fling you across the level, and whole rooms slide in from off-screen; position becomes a consequence of a decision rather than the decision itself.

**The board is not one kind of block.** Two shades of red that look identical on screen and only count against their own kind; pegs you may hop over that are never captured, sitting among pegs that are; a yellow button that drives a grey platform. Pieces that look alike behave differently, and you find out by touching them — that is the direct cure for "blocky."

**Someone else is working.** A helper on the far side of an uncrossable line hauls loose crates to the delivery floor, one step for every key you press, and a thief does the same in reverse — lifting crates out of your hands and off floor you already finished. Nothing is banked until the last crate lands and the thief is gone.

**The game never answers.** The rune game's move budget is roomy — roughly double what a good solve costs. What kills guessing is silence: no tick on a correct tile, no partial credit, no warmer-or-colder. The board says nothing until the whole line is right at once, then simply ends.

# The Sokoban verdict

Plenty is left. The verb was never the problem — the solitaire is. A room where nothing else wants anything has one plan, worked out once and then typed in. The proven fix is cheap: a barrier that stops people but not cargo, a worker on the far side who delivers on your clock, a rival who undoes you, and at least one level with no delivery floor on your side at all so the hand-off is mandatory. That's a level-design pass on games we already have. What we should stop shipping is the fiftieth empty room of crates and marked squares.

# Five things to do next

1. Put a helper and a thief across an uncrossable line in our three best push-block games, with one level we cannot finish alone.
2. Strip all partial feedback out of one game and see whether it still plays — if guessing dies and reading survives, do it everywhere.
3. Cap every game at six controls, then give one control a second meaning that arrives mid-game, and check a fresh player finds it unaided.
4. Print the win condition onto the pieces as a live readout that lights and unlights as you move — then three levels in, rub it off everything but the piece in hand.
5. Give failure a performance instead of a message: a beat where nothing happens, then the board reacting, then a control we have never seen arriving on screen.
